title: Continuous quality — requirements and the tests that verify them
note: Each requirement names the golden tests that verify it. traceability.mjs checks this file against what actually ran: a requirement with no test, a test id that does not exist, and a named test that did not pass are all failures. A table nobody checks is a table that rots.

requirements.statement: A pipeline can run QA NXT from a command line and act on the result without parsing output.
Every documented exit code can actually be produced, and each distinguishes who should look at the failure.
A run publishes evidence whether it passed or failed.
A failure is reported with enough context to act on without opening the platform.
A run records where it came from, so a failure can be traced to the commit and the deployment that produced it.
API endpoints can be tested as first-class test cases, in the same engine as UI tests.
An API contract change is detected against a stored baseline and classified by how badly it breaks callers.
A UI failure caused by an API call is explained as such, rather than as a broken locator.
A change selects the tests it reaches, and says why each was or was not selected.
Regression runs happen on a schedule without anybody asking, and a schedule that stops running says so.
A quality gate produces PASS, FAIL or REVIEW, and REVIEW survives to the pipeline as its own answer.
A quality gate rule whose metric this run could not measure is reported as unmeasured, never as satisfied.
A release decision can be made from what changed, not only from what is broken.
Coverage that stops being exercised is visible rather than silently dropped.
A failure is told to whoever configured a channel, and whether they were told is recorded.
Notifications never carry a credential, checked against the bytes sent.
Test data is reproducible from a seed, so a failure can be reproduced.
A credential is never stored as a literal in test data, and is never returned by any read.
Accessibility is measured against named rules, and a clean result is not reported as a clearance.
A team can measure accessibility before enforcing it.
Visual changes are detected against a baseline, with a noise floor that does not produce false differences.
A visual difference asks for a person by default rather than failing the build, and what was masked is on the record.
QA NXT never tests outside its configured authorization boundary, and production is refused without an explicit written authorization.
A security refusal is reported distinctly from a permissions failure, so nobody resolves it by widening access.
A run is never silently finished twice, and one occurrence of a schedule starts exactly one run.
Every continuous-quality surface is scoped to one tenant, and a denial is accompanied by the owner's successful read.
The audit trail can be read through the product, is scoped to one organization, and no parameter widens it.
Actions that change what the platform will permit — authorizing production, changing a schedule, changing a quality gate — are recorded with who asked and why.
A failed or refused action is recorded as such rather than omitted, and never carries the credential that was attempted.
One correlation id follows a request from the caller through the API and the queue to the execution and the audit record, and a caller cannot abuse it.
Liveness and readiness are separable, so a dependency outage does not present as a dead process.
A model provider that fails — by timing out, erroring, or answering unusably — fails the request visibly and never causes a fabricated result.
Model output is data and never instruction: schema-valid output carrying injected commands reaches no test as an action.
Deterministic execution is independent of the model: a provider outage does not stop a test run, and every model failure is recorded with its reason.
